issues.item: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For a toxic chemical exposure trauma, a weapons-related visual trigger is hard to reconcile clinically unless there is evidence of a separate assault or combat-related trauma. The other trigger items (loss of autonomy, being watched) could occur in medical, workplace, or contamination-related contexts, but weapons specifically points to a qualitatively different trauma context and is therefore not coherent with the stated trauma type.

vignette: Theresa, a 44-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and tattoo artist, experienced a traumatic event that has profoundly impacted her life. Six months ago, Theresa was exposed to toxic chemicals at work when an unmarked container in the studio released fumes. She was forced into a small room without ventilation while attempting to secure the area for safety, a moment she now vividly recalls as an intense loss of autonomy and feeling suffocated. Since then, Theresa has found herself frequently triggered by situations that remind her of this experience. One of the most potent triggers is the antiseptic smell, reminiscent of the chemicals in the studio. When she visits the hospital for regular health checks, the antiseptic odor immediately transports her back to that small, suffocating room. This connection has made her reluctant to seek medical care, fearing another episode where she might feel trapped and helpless again. Moreover, Theresa's sense of being watched is heightened in public spaces. As a tattoo artist, her work often involves interacting with clients who sit still for long periods while getting their tattoos. She feels particularly uneasy when clients are observing her closely during sessions, as if they are scrutinizing every move she makes. This feeling intensifies the sense of loss of autonomy and reactivates the trauma. Her husband has noticed a change in her behavior over time. Theresa avoids crowded areas and often cancels social engagements, preferring to stay home where she feels more secure and less watched. Even within the comfort of her own studio, she finds it difficult to concentrate when clients are present, leading to longer sessions that both exhaust her and frustrate her customers. Despite these challenges, what finally brought Theresa to seek help was a recent incident at work. A new client, who smelled faintly of antiseptic from a recent doctor's visit, triggered a severe panic attack in Theresa while she was working on his tattoo. She had to stop mid-session and leave the studio in tears, deeply embarrassed and ashamed. Theresa is most afraid that her symptoms will worsen, leaving her unable to work or engage with others at all. She hopes that therapy can help her regain control over her life and reduce these overwhelming triggers so she can continue working as a tattoo artist without feeling constantly under threat.
